title: Volvox is a green ball of up to 50,000 cells, with its offspring growing inside

cover.alt: A Volvox colony under the microscope: a translucent green sphere studded with tiny cells, with darker green clusters inside.

body: *Volvox* is a green alga that lives as a hollow sphere of up to **50,000 cells**, each with two flagella pointing outwards. The cells beat in a coordinated way, and an eyespot at the front lets the colony swim towards light. Most of the cells never reproduce. That job falls to a few large cells inside, which divide again and again to build new colonies within the parent.

slides.alt: Microscope footage of a Volvox colony: a green sphere covered in tiny dot-like cells turns slowly, and as the focus shifts darker green clusters show inside it.
slides.caption: A Volvox colony turns under the microscope. As the focus moves from its surface of tiny cells to its middle, the darker green clusters inside come into view.
slides.music: “Mana Two - Part 2” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: How a colony makes a colony

steps.label: A large reproductive cell sits inside
The embryo, inside out, turns itself right
A daughter colony forms within the parent

left.label: Body cells
left.text: Small cells in a single layer on the surface, each with two flagella. They swim, but never reproduce.

right.label: Reproductive cells
right.text: A few large cells in the interior that cannot swim. They divide to build the next generation.

slides.question: About how many million years ago did Volvox's line split from single-celled ancestors?
slides.explanation: About 200 million years ago. Since then its colonies have split the work: body cells to swim, a few big cells to reproduce.

slides.clue: The Latin verb meaning 'to roll' that gave Volvox its name
slides.detail: The name joins volvere, 'to roll', with -ox, 'fierce'. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first reported seeing Volvox in 1700.
